Modeling time-series data

Michael Barkasi

2025-10-11

tutorial_timeseries.Rmd

Introduction

Wisps naturally model between-group effects describable as two-valued categorical factors, e.g., comparing controls vs a treatment or male vs female. Coarse-grain comparisons over time, such as young vs old or postnatal day PXPX vs postnatal day PYPY, can be shoehorned into this framework. However, it’s often desirable to model longer time series TT.

Time series as factor series

While wisps are limited to binary covariate fixed-effect factors ξ\xi, i.e., ξ∈{0,1}\xi\in\{0,1\}, the number of factor levels can be increased to accommodate more time points by modeling time factors ξT\xi_T as an ordered series of factors ξTm\xi_{T_m} with additive effects βTm\beta_{T_m}. Given a series of time points: T1<T2<⋯<TnT_1 < T_2 < \cdots < T_n a corresponding time-factor series ξT\xi_T is defined with nn ordinal binary factors: ξT1<ξT2<⋯<ξTn\xi_{T_1} < \xi_{T_2} < \cdots < \xi_{T_n} For binary factors ξ\xi with corresponding effect term β\beta, the effect on a model parameter zz is: z↦z+β+interaction termsz \mapsto z + \beta + \text{interaction terms} To achieve the cumulative effect of time, the effect of a time factor ξTm\xi_{T_m}, for m≤nm\leq n, is given by summing the series of effects βTi\beta_{T_i} from time factors ξTi\xi_{T_i} for Ti≤TmT_i\leq T_m: z↦z+∑i=1mβTi+interaction termsz \mapsto z + \sum_{i=1}^{m} \beta_{T_i} + \text{interaction terms} Wispack implements this cumulative effect by defining the effect of ξT\xi_T to be: z↦z+∑i=1nβTiξTi+interaction termsz \mapsto z + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \beta_{T_i}\xi_{T_i} + \text{interaction terms} and stipulating, for each sampled data point ss, that if ξTm(s)=1\xi_{T_m}(s)=1 then ξTi(s)=1\xi_{T_i}(s)=1 for all i<mi<m.

Demo data

This tutorial will use MERFISH data collected from the auditory cortex of mice and preprocessed into laminar coordinates as described in the introductory tutorial (see also this preprint). As with all data appropriate for wispack and in line with well-known modeling functions in R (e.g., lm(), lmer()), the data must be in long format. That is, each row must correspond to a single observation, which when modeling spatial transcriptomics data will typically be a count of transcripts from an RNA species in a single cell.

countdata <- read.csv(
  system.file(
      "extdata", 
      "ACx_laminar_countdata_demo.csv", 
      package = "wispack"
    )
  )

print(head(countdata))
##   count bin context   gene mouse hemisphere age
## 1     0  96  cortex Bcl11b     1       left  12
## 2     0  95  cortex Bcl11b     1       left  12
## 3     0  98  cortex Bcl11b     1       left  12
## 4     0 100  cortex Bcl11b     1       left  12
## 5     0  99  cortex Bcl11b     1       left  12
## 6     0  99  cortex Bcl11b     1       left  12

As in the introductory tutorial, the data used here includes a dummy context variable filled with “cortex”, a variable giving the hemisphere (left vs right) of each observation, and counts (by cell) for the following six layer specific genes:

print(unique(countdata$gene))
## [1] "Bcl11b" "Fezf2"  "Satb2"  "Nxph3"  "Cux2"   "Rorb"

However, the data used in the introductory tutorial was collected from four mice of only two distinct ages: P12 and P18. This tutorial includes data from these original four mice, plus a fifth mouse at age P7.

for (m in unique(countdata$mouse)) {
  cat(
    paste0(
      "Mouse ", m, 
      " is age P", unique(countdata$age[countdata$mouse==m]), 
      "\n"
    )
  )
}
## Mouse 1 is age P12
## Mouse 2 is age P18
## Mouse 3 is age P7
## Mouse 4 is age P12
## Mouse 5 is age P18

Modeling time series in wispack

The parts of a wisp model must be defined, relative to the column names of the data. Wispack expects columns for the count to be modeled (count), the spatial coordinate (bin), the context (e.g., brain region, context), the species being counted (e.g., gene, species), and the random effect factor (ran). As the data includes explicit count and bin columns, these do not need to be redefined. As the names are different, wispack does need to be told that the RNA species data is included in the gene column and the random effect factor is given by the mouse column. It would be natural to use the celltype_MMC column as the context, but as this tutorial is focused on time series modeling, the context will be set to a constant value of “cortex” for all data points. Finally, the time series factor will be defined as the age column.

# Define variables in the dataframe for the model
data.variables <- list(
    species = "gene",
    ran = "mouse",
    timeseries = "age",
    fixedeffects = c("hemisphere", "age")
  )

Let’s model the time-dependent lateralization of layer-specific gene expression of the auditory cortex of developing mice. Hence, hemisphere and age will be fixed-effect factors.

# Define fixed effects to test
fixed.effect.names <- c("hemisphere", "age")
